newsitem.title: USA: Wet fields delay Oklahoma winter wheat harvest.
newsitem.headline: Wet fields delay Oklahoma winter wheat harvest.

text.p: Wet fields helped delay wheat harvesting in Oklahoma during the week ended Sunday, the state's agricultural statistics service said Monday in its weekly crop progress report.
"Green sucker heads and rain are major culprits in the harvest delay. Producers are anxiously awaiting warm, dry weather in order to start combining fields," the report said.

Harvesting ranged from none in the Panhandle district to 29 percent in southwest Oklahoma. Statewide, wheat was only seven percent harvested, lagging 60 percent last year and 29 percent for the five-year average.

The state's wheat was rated seven percent very poor, 100 poor, 28 fair, 52 good and three percent excellent. A week ago, the crop was rated six percent very poor, 10 poor, 30 fair, 51 good and three percent excellent.

Only one percent of the state's corn was tasseling, against nil last week, 13 percent last year and 12 on average. Soybeans were 68 percent planted, against 65 last week, 87 last year and 61 percent on average.
Sorghum acreage was 40 percent planted, against 24 last week, 58 percent last year and 69 percent on average.

The moisture has improved range and pasture conditions, and one source in southwest Oklahoma rated this year's pasture as probably the best in eight to 10 years. Statewide, condition was rated two percent poor, 18 percent fair, 65 percent good and 15 percent excellent.
